title: Binary Trees: Level-Order Traversal (BFS)
oneLiner: Visit every node one whole depth-level at a time, using a queue instead of recursion.
keyTakeaway: Breadth-first search explores level by level using a QUEUE (FIFO): push the root, then repeatedly pop a node, visit it, and push its children -- because a queue preserves order, every node at depth d (d steps below the root) gets pushed (and therefore visited) before any node at depth d+1. That queue-driven shape is the actual difference from DFS, not just "a different order to write down" -- DFS's recursion IS an implicit stack (dive all the way down one path before backtracking), while BFS explicitly needs a queue to fan out level by level instead.
explanation: Start with a queue containing just the root. Then loop: pop the front of the queue, record its value, and push its (non-null) children onto the BACK of the queue. Because a queue is FIFO, nodes come out in the exact order they were discovered -- which is level by level, left to right within each level, since every node at one depth gets queued before any node one level deeper. This is the queue lesson (Queues: Simulate Enqueue/Dequeue) applied directly: BFS IS "enqueue children, dequeue and process," repeated until the queue empties. Watch out for the classic mix-up with DFS: reaching for recursion here would naturally produce a depth-first order (preorder, most likely) instead, since recursive calls use the call stack, not a queue -- BFS specifically needs an explicit queue data structure, it's not just "traversal, but organized differently."

visualizationSteps.message: Queue = [root]. Dequeue a node, record it, enqueue its children -- repeat until the queue is empty.
Dequeue 5, record it. Enqueue its children: [3, 8].
Dequeue 3, record it. Enqueue its children: [1, 4].
Dequeue 8, record it. Enqueue its children: [7, 9].
Dequeue 1, record it. No children to enqueue.
Dequeue 4, record it. No children to enqueue.
Dequeue 7, record it. No children to enqueue.
Dequeue 9, record it. No children to enqueue.
Queue is empty -- done. Level order: [5, 3, 8, 1, 4, 7, 9].

recognitionSignals: The problem cares about DEPTH or LEVEL specifically -- "shortest path," "minimum number of steps," "nodes at distance k."
You need to process things in the order they were discovered, level by level, rather than diving deep into one branch first.
gotchas: Using a stack (or recursion, which implicitly uses the call stack) instead of a queue silently produces a depth-first order, not breadth-first -- same-looking code, wrong traversal shape.
Forgetting to check for null children before pushing them onto the queue crashes (or corrupts the traversal) the same way forgetting a base case does in DFS.

If you need to know WHICH level a node belongs to (not just the flat visit order), you have to explicitly track how many nodes were in the queue at the start of each level -- the queue itself doesn't remember level boundaries for you.
confusableWith: Binary Trees: Inorder Traversal (DFS) (this track) visits every node too, but dives fully into the left subtree before ever looking at a sibling -- the tell is whether the problem cares about DEPTH-first order (DFS) or LEVEL-first order (BFS).

complexity.note: Every node is enqueued and dequeued once; the queue can hold a whole level, which for a complete tree is about n/2 nodes -- O(n).
